title: Respiratory Case Review
summary: Review spatial, clinical and physiological evidence in a synthetic respiratory presentation. Training simulation—not clinical guidance.

mission.role: You are the trainee reviewing a rapidly deteriorating respiratory presentation.
mission.objective: Reconstruct the affected airway location, track the deterioration and decide what the evidence requires.
deliverables: Commit to the location of the dominant finding
Update the differential as evidence arrives
Cite the evidence supporting the conclusion

patient.label: Case C — synthetic patient
patient.presentingComplaint: Rapidly worsening breathlessness and difficulty completing sentences after several days of coryzal symptoms.
history: Episodes of variable wheeze and nocturnal cough have occurred previously.
Several preventer doses were missed this week.
Reliever benefit has become brief and incomplete over the last six hours.

findings.label: Diffuse wall thickening with mild narrowing
findings.description: The airway wall appears diffusely thickened, with mild reduction in the visible lumen.
findings.significance: This supports a widespread airway process but does not explain the acute trajectory alone.

findings.label: Dominant posterior basal mucus plug
findings.description: A dominant mucus plug substantially occludes the posterior basal segmental lumen.
findings.significance: This is the dominant spatial finding to localise; it supports obstruction but is not the sole basis for the conclusion.

differential.label: Severe asthma exacerbation
differential.description: Variable airway symptoms with acute physiological deterioration.

differential.label: COPD exacerbation
differential.description: Acute airflow limitation in the context of chronic obstructive disease.

differential.label: Lobar pneumonia
differential.description: Focal pulmonary infection as the primary explanation.

differential.label: Pulmonary embolism
differential.description: Acute vascular obstruction as the primary explanation.

content.heading: Six-hour change
content.body: Previous variable wheeze and nocturnal cough are followed by rapidly worsening breathlessness, incomplete reliever response and difficulty completing sentences.

content.title: Peak expiratory flow trend
content.summary: Peak expiratory flow falls from 310 to 170 L/min over six hours.

content.alt: Illustration of a bronchiole leading into alveolar ducts and alveoli.
content.caption: Use the branching conducting-airway anatomy to distinguish lobe, segment and structure.

content.alt: Histology image of an inflamed bronchiole with mucoid material narrowing the lumen.
content.caption: Reference image showing airway-wall change and mucoid luminal obstruction.

stages.title: Orient
stages.purpose: Reconstruct where the dominant obstruction sits before interpreting its clinical importance.
stages.intro: Trace the airway, inspect the dominant finding, then localise it without an overlay.

update.narrative: Breathlessness has worsened rapidly after several days of coryzal symptoms.

content.prompt: Starting in the mid trachea, follow the airway to the right lower lobe and inspect the dominant posterior basal obstruction.
Localise the dominant obstruction from lobe to segment and structure.

options.label: Posterior basal segment
Superior segment
Lateral basal segment
Segmental bronchus
Pulmonary artery branch
Visceral pleura

content.explanation: The traversed route enters the right lower lobe, posterior basal segment and its conducting segmental bronchus.

stages.title: Observe
stages.purpose: Identify the observations that establish the direction and severity of change.
stages.intro: Select the observations that indicate marked deterioration.

update.narrative: Reliever benefit is brief, speech is limited and objective respiratory observations are worsening.

content.prompt: Which findings support marked respiratory deterioration? Select all that apply.

options.label: Difficulty completing sentences
Serial expiratory flow has fallen substantially
Oxygen saturation is low and continuing to fall
Carbon dioxide has risen during ongoing distress
Previous nocturnal cough by itself
Coryzal symptoms by themselves

content.explanation: Speech limitation, falling expiratory flow, hypoxaemia and a rising PaCO₂ during distress all add severity information; the background symptoms alone do not grade the acute episode.

content.prompt: Rate each working hypothesis after reviewing the deterioration.

stages.title: Interpret
stages.purpose: Explain what the changing physiology means when read with the whole trajectory.
stages.intro: Explain the carbon-dioxide trend in the context of the other observations.

update.narrative: Falling flow and oxygenation now accompany a rising carbon-dioxide trend.

content.prompt: Why is the PaCO₂ rise concerning in this presentation?

options.label: It may indicate that ventilation is failing to keep pace with the work of breathing
It confirms recovery because PaCO₂ has returned toward the reference range
It measures oxygenation only and does not inform ventilation
It is more consistent with improving airflow obstruction

content.explanation: A distressed patient may initially lower PaCO₂ through hyperventilation; a subsequent rise alongside worsening flow and hypoxaemia can indicate reduced ventilatory reserve.

content.prompt: Revise each hypothesis after interpreting the serial physiology.

stages.title: Diagnose
stages.purpose: Cite the decisive evidence, commit to the leading explanation and identify its consequence.
stages.intro: Synthesize the pattern, then identify its immediate consequence.

update.narrative: The complete history, serial physiology and spatial finding are available for synthesis.

content.prompt: Which reviewed evidence makes the leading conclusion most defensible?
content.explanation: The prior pattern, serial deterioration and inspected obstruction jointly support the conclusion.

content.prompt: Which diagnosis best fits the complete pattern?

options.label: Severe asthma exacerbation with deteriorating ventilatory reserve
COPD exacerbation with a chronic obstructive pattern
Lobar pneumonia with a focal infection pattern
Pulmonary embolism with an acute vascular pattern

content.explanation: Prior variable symptoms, worsening expiratory flow, hypoxaemia and the PaCO₂ trajectory converge on a severe asthma exacerbation with diminishing ventilatory reserve.

content.prompt: What immediate consequence follows from this synthesis?

options.label: Treat the pattern as high-risk deterioration and activate urgent escalation under the local emergency pathway
Continue close observation and schedule reassessment
Obtain another peak-flow measurement before deciding whether to escalate
Prioritize the focal airway finding when selecting the immediate response

content.explanation: The combined clinical and physiological pattern warrants urgent escalation; neither a near-reference PaCO₂ nor one spatial finding should be interpreted in isolation.

expertBenchmark.name: Authored respiratory-educator benchmark

rationales.exac-explore-airway: The authored route reaches the posterior basal segment and inspects the dominant mucus occlusion.
rationales.exac-localise: The finding lies in the right lower lobe posterior basal segmental bronchus.
rationales.exac-severity-signals: Each selected item contributes acute severity information rather than disease identity alone.
rationales.exac-differential-observe: The initial ratings preserve competing acute explanations while recognising the deteriorating airway pattern.
rationales.exac-co2-reasoning: The trend is interpreted with work of breathing, flow and oxygenation rather than against a reference interval in isolation.
rationales.exac-differential-interpret: The revised ratings show how the serial physiology changes the relative likelihoods.
rationales.exac-cite-evidence: The cited history, serial physiology and inspected obstruction support the high-risk synthesis.
rationales.exac-best-diagnosis: Variable airway symptoms and the acute objective trajectory form the most coherent synthesis.
rationales.exac-immediate-consequence: The combined deterioration signals justify urgent escalation through the applicable emergency pathway.

path.label: Trace and localise the obstruction
path.detail: Follow the right lower-lobe route, inspect the dominant mucus plug and localise it to the posterior basal segmental bronchus.

path.label: Grade the deterioration
path.detail: Prioritise speech limitation, falling expiratory flow, hypoxaemia and the rising PaCO₂ trend.

path.label: Interpret physiology in context
path.detail: Read the PaCO₂ rise alongside worsening work of breathing, flow and oxygenation rather than in isolation.

path.label: Synthesize diagnosis and consequence
path.detail: Combine the variable-airway history and objective trajectory, then identify the need for urgent escalation.

evidenceWeights.note: Variable prior symptoms plus abrupt worsening establish the disease pattern and acuity.
The serial decline supplies objective evidence of worsening airflow limitation.
Hypoxaemia and rising PaCO₂ during distress indicate diminishing ventilatory reserve.
The anatomy reference supports accurate route tracing and localisation.
The inspected focal obstruction adds spatial pathology but does not determine the diagnosis alone.

expertBenchmark.diagnosisRationale: Prior variable airway symptoms, rapidly falling expiratory flow, hypoxaemia and a rising PaCO₂ during ongoing distress converge on severe asthma exacerbation with diminishing ventilatory reserve. The focal mucus plug supports the obstructive picture but must not be interpreted alone.

debrief.summary: The spatial task identified a dominant posterior basal mucus obstruction against diffuse airway-wall change. The diagnostic task kept disease identity separate from severity, then integrated falling flow, hypoxaemia and a rising PaCO₂ into a high-risk deterioration pattern.

keyEvidence.why: Speech limitation and the variable-airway history distinguish disease pattern from acute severity.
The serial fall to 170 L/min makes the deterioration objective and changes the urgency of interpretation.
Falling oxygen saturation and rising PaCO₂ during distress signal reduced ventilatory reserve.
The branching reference supports route tracing and precise lobe-to-structure localisation.
Inspecting the dominant posterior basal mucus plug connects the endoscopic route to the localisation task.
